question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what probe orientation adjustment is being performed, and what is the imaging objective?
A. Slight counterclockwise obliquing while angling down to align the target organ’s long axis
B. Slide the probe laterally while maintaining the same orientation to use an adjacent organ as an acoustic window and reduce bowel gas artifact.
C. Slight clockwise rotation with a gentle heel-toe to obtain a true short-axis (transverse) view of the target organ.
D. Angle the probe cephalad without rotation to center the organ’s head region and optimize visualization of nearby vessels with color Doppler.
groundtruth: The operator places the probe high in the epigastrium, angles it inferiorly, and obliques slightly counterclockwise to better align the imaging plane with the pancreatic axis.
original_question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what probe orientation adjustment is being performed, and what is the imaging objective?
A. Slide the probe laterally while maintaining the same orientation to use an adjacent organ as an acoustic window and reduce bowel gas artifact.
B. Angle the probe cephalad without rotation to center the organ’s head region and optimize visualization of nearby vessels with color Doppler.
C. Slight clockwise rotation with a gentle heel-toe to obtain a true short-axis (transverse) view of the target organ.
D. Slight counterclockwise obliquing while angling down to align the target organ’s long axis

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: C
Explanation: The observed probe movement is slight clockwise rotation paired with gentle heel-toe manipulation. The resulting ultrasound view shows rounded, ovoid cross-sections of vascular/ductal structures consistent with a transverse (short-axis) orientation, confirming the objective is obtaining a true short-axis view of the target organ.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what scanning strategy is being used, and why?
A. Sliding the probe along the skin to keep a similar plane while relocating to center a target structure, not to ensure full organ coverage.
B. Fanning/tilting the probe in place to interrogate a focal area in multiple planes to optimize a specific finding.
C. Performing a continuous sweep through the organ to ensure full coverage
D. Capturing sequential static images at set intervals to document key anatomic landmarks rather than sweeping continuously.
groundtruth: The operator sweeps through the entire pancreas rather than capturing static images of only the splenic vein, ensuring full anatomic coverage to avoid missing pathology on a single slice.
original_question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what scanning strategy is being used, and why?
A. Fanning/tilting the probe in place to interrogate a focal area in multiple planes to optimize a specific finding.
B. Sliding the probe along the skin to keep a similar plane while relocating to center a target structure, not to ensure full organ coverage.
C. Capturing sequential static images at set intervals to document key anatomic landmarks rather than sweeping continuously.
D. Performing a continuous sweep through the organ to ensure full coverage

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: B
The probe is fanned/tilted in a fixed position on the skin, repeatedly viewing the focal area initially marked by the green arrow from multiple imaging angles. This is done to optimize visualization of the specific targeted finding in that region, rather than performing a full organ sweep, sliding to relocate the probe, or capturing only static interval images.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what gross probe motion pattern is being performed, and what is the goal of that movement?
A. Fanning/rocking the probe through the organ in place to interrogate its depth and look for focal lesions.
B. Rotating the probe about 90° to obtain an orthogonal (short-axis/transverse) view for anatomic confirmation.
C. A systematic sweep along the organ’s length to cover it end-to-end
D. Sliding the probe slightly to bring an adjacent landmark organ or vessel into the same window to verify orientation.
groundtruth: The operator scans along the pancreas from the head/uncinate region through to the tail to visualize the full length of pancreatic anatomy.
original_question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what gross probe motion pattern is being performed, and what is the goal of that movement?
A. Rotating the probe about 90° to obtain an orthogonal (short-axis/transverse) view for anatomic confirmation.
B. A systematic sweep along the organ’s length to cover it end-to-end
C. Sliding the probe slightly to bring an adjacent landmark organ or vessel into the same window to verify orientation.
D. Fanning/rocking the probe through the organ in place to interrogate its depth and look for focal lesions.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
The probe is being fanned/rocked in place (no lateral sliding of the probe footprint across the skin) to obtain sequential cross-sectional slices through the imaged area, allowing interrogation of the full depth of the structure to identify any focal lesions. Other options are incorrect: there is no 90-degree rotation, no end-to-end sweep along the organ length, and no sliding to bring adjacent structures into view.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what is being measured with on-screen calipers, and what is the clinical intent?
A. Duct caliber to assess for dilatation
B. Portal vein diameter to screen for portal hypertension
C. Gallbladder wall thickness to evaluate for acute cholecystitis
D. Inferior vena cava diameter to estimate intravascular volume status
groundtruth: The operator visualizes the pancreatic duct and assesses its diameter, using a normal cutoff of about 2 mm to help determine whether the duct is dilated.
original_question:

B. Duct caliber to assess for dilatation
C. Inferior vena cava diameter to estimate intravascular volume status

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: C
The on-screen caliper is measuring the thickness of the gallbladder wall, as seen by the measurement spanning the tissue layer superficial to the anechoic gallbladder lumen. Evaluation of gallbladder wall thickness (a value >3mm is abnormal) is a standard step in assessing for acute cholecystitis.

question:

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what probe maneuver is performed after identifying a tubular target, and what is the purpose?
A. Slide the probe to center an adjacent artery/vein to use as a landmark for orientation before further evaluation.
B. Apply graded compression over the structure to assess compressibility and tenderness at the point of maximal pain.
C. Rotating to align long-axis with the tube to elongate it and follow its course
D. Turn on color Doppler while keeping the same plane to confirm whether the tubular structure is vascular.
groundtruth: After finding the common bile duct, the operator rotates the probe to be sagittal relative to the duct, elongating it to trace its course toward the liver.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what major plane change is being performed, and what does it accomplish?
A. Fanning/rocking the probe to sweep through the organ while staying in the same imaging plane to survey its extent.
B. Sliding (translating) the probe to a neighboring window to reacquire the organ without changing the imaging plane.
C. A 90° rotation to obtain short-axis (transverse) images of the organ
D. Angling/heel-toeing the probe to align with the organ’s true long axis and minimize foreshortening.
groundtruth: The operator rotates the probe 90 degrees into a sagittal plane relative to the patient’s body to obtain transverse (short-axis) images of the pancreas.
original_question:
[MCQ] Based on the video clip, what major plane change is being performed, and what does it accomplish?
A. Angling/heel-toeing the probe to align with the organ’s true long axis and minimize foreshortening.
B. A 90° rotation to obtain short-axis (transverse) images of the organ
C. Fanning/rocking the probe to sweep through the organ while staying in the same imaging plane to survey its extent.
D. Sliding (translating) the probe to a neighboring window to reacquire the organ without changing the imaging plane.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
The observed probe movement is fanning/rocking: the probe is tilted back and forth to sweep the ultrasound beam through the organ while maintaining the same imaging plane orientation, allowing full survey of the organ's extent. The other options are incorrect: there is no sliding of the probe to a new window, no 90° rotation to switch to short axis, and no heel-toe angling performed to align specifically to the organ's long axis.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: C
The vertebral body (spine) is the most posterior structure among the options, appearing as a hyperechoic (bright) posterior landmark with associated acoustic shadowing, which serves as the consistent posterior reference to confirm position during the transverse abdominal sweep. question:
